title: A New Dawn For Mathematical Progress
content: In the past few months, unreleased frontier AI systems have significantly disrupted a classic conception of mathematics. They successfully established a complete formalization of Andrew Wiles’s proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem, found a solution to the Navier-Stokes problem and — just a few days ago — generated hundreds of manuscripts that each purport to prove an important mathematical problem. Most recently, on October 26, another of the Clay Millennium Prize problems was felled by an AI system.

title: Turbulent Times Call For Experimental Law
content:
MUNICH — Shortly after wandering into the Munich Urban Colab this summer, I found myself trying to follow an intense conversation in German about the city’s new experiment with autonomous buses. A local official, clocking my curious puzzlement, offered an aside in English: “We are asking ourselves: ‘What does it mean when the law is an experiment too?’”

No question may be more essential to governance in our era of dangerous uncertainty. 

Global warming is accelerating faster than global treaties on mitigation can be negotiated. Climate catastrophes occur with a sudden ferocity beyond what current adaptation laws anticipate. Biological threats surface and kill before public health responses can be formulated. And AI is evolving faster and more wildly than regulators or lawmakers, or even its designers, expect.

All this dizzying unpredictability is undermining traditional legal structures. The threat is not just to the rule of law, but to the very nature of law, at least as humans have conceived it.

title: The Sediment Of Culture Shapes Political Order
content:
As a global journal of ideas, Noema receives feedback from readers all over the world that broadens our way of seeing and kindles the further iteration of our thinking. One recent case is a response by Carl Gay, an executive of the Cloudspago consultancy in Australia, to the Noema essay “When The Present Eats The Future: The Achilles Heel of Consumer Democracies.”

In that essay, I contrast post-Mao China’s capacity for reaching a consensus on long-term goals and determinedly implementing them over many years without a break in continuity with the increasing inability of consumer democracies to do so. The example I used in the context of climate change was how China set the goal decades ago of dominating green technology, especially electric vehicles and batteries, and has steadily achieved that objective, while most open societies of the West have sputtered behind. Its “whole dragon” approach brings the resources of the entire system to bear on the challenge at hand.

title: Noema’s AI Reading List
content:
AI’s climb up the capability ladder is moving more rapidly, even exponentially, than its progenitors expected. To keep up and put it in perspective, Noema has compiled a reading list of our best essays and interviews from a couple of years ago through the present. No doubt, we will need a new list again a few months down the road.

For now, here is a resource for following the trajectory of the most important technological breakthrough of this century so far.

1. How To Future-Proof Your Career In The Age Of AI

The most prized workers will be those who can decode a sea of outputs, spot the meaningful signal and translate it into action that others understand and trust.

by Nils Gilman

2. Whose AI Will Rule The World

As AI changes everything, the Chinese seem more optimistic than the Americans. Why?

by Jacob Dreyer

3. How AI Will Change Us

When the most patient, well-read, emotionally responsive conversationalist in the world is always available, what will we still need from one another?

by Houda Nait El Barj

4. AI Could Actually Help Rebuild The Middle Class

AI doesn’t have to be a job destroyer. It offers us the opportunity to extend expertise to a larger set of workers.

by David Autor

title: Sudan As A Mirror For Today’s World
content:
Sudan has often served as a mirror for judging the health of the liberal world order because it has repeatedly been a laboratory for multilateral interventions to prevent atrocities and stabilize the humanitarian situation.

During the second Sudanese civil war, which stretched from 1983 to 2005, an estimated more than two million people died. In Darfur during the first decade of the 2000s, international observers estimated that 300,000 people died and another 2-3 million people were displaced.

At the time, finding a solution to Sudan’s conflicts was a priority for the United States and the coalitions it galvanized. For instance, Sudan’s second civil war came to an end only after intense mediation by the troika of the United States, the United Kingdom and Norway, as well as Sudan’s African neighbors, in 2005.  The level of Western concern and diplomatic resources mobilized to intervene in Sudan’s conflicts in the early 2000s feels almost unimaginable today.

title: When The Present Eats The Future
content:
The Achilles heel of consumer democracies is that there is precious little constituency for the future in the present. All the feedback signals — in politics, culture and the market — are geared to short-term gratification. In each case, the incentives of the system deliver what the most influential demographic wants, and when they want it, which is now.

From fast fashion to electoral contests to quarterly earnings reports, the system is responsive to the pursuit of happiness defined by the near horizon.

The consequence of this, which Harvard sociologist Daniel Bell argued more than half a century ago in his book, “The Cultural Contradictions of Capitalism,” is that the present ends up eating the future to the detriment of the long-term sustainability of society. The recent Noema essay by Simon Curtis and Ian Klaus titled “Americans Are Losing The Long Game” is excellent on this point.

title: What We Can Save In A Time Of Endings
content:
HAPPISBURGH, England — Off the coast of Norfolk on edge of the North Sea, the ocean can seem calm, but the waters are deceptive. Beneath the marbled brown, lie sand banks and submerged mountains waiting to ensnare unsuspecting ships. Happisburgh (pronounced Hays-burro) is a small, pretty town, its narrow roads lined by houses with walls made of flint pressed into mortar. The beach roads all have names like Stone’s Throw or Cliff Top, and the sea has always been present in people’s lives. But inching ever closer for years, now its incursions are rapid and frightening.

The light changed suddenly. Over my shoulder, the sky was dark with rain that towered in hazy columns against a thunderous glow. It rolled over the beach, over the houses, falling into the sea, billowing over the crumbling cliff edge. Lightning split the blackness, and the clouds rumbled. Gulls soared like scraps of loose paper, and sand martins wheeled in a frenzy, seeking refuge. For a moment, the world had ended. Then, it was clear again: sun shining, birds calling, people laughing.

title: An Inside Look At How To Tame Unstoppable AI
content:
Earlier this year, a university decided to audit the effectiveness of its new AI system designed to help answer student questions. So, university officials hired me, an AI auditor, to come take a look. During my review, I discovered that the AI agent, which was supposed to handle only general questions about the academic calendar and organizational matters, had started opening students’ personal records — accessing data that wasn’t needed to answer their questions. The chatbot, however, did nothing further with that information.

When the university’s engineers, at the time, learned what happened from the access logs, they fixed it, and that was that. There was no official record. No internal rule required them to record such incidents, and nobody was assigned to track events like this. It was simply part of the engineering team’s bug-fixing process. The incident was what I call a near miss, and near misses are what a reporting system exists to catch. The same behavior could lead to something more serious next time, and we only know about this case because the university voluntarily brought me in to examine the system.

title: We Are Already Post-Human
content:
From Silicon Valley to the Vatican, across kitchen tables and in the halls of power, the world is astir over the question of whether humans will be able to control the AIs we’ve created. But that begs the question: What does it mean to be “human”?

One place to start sorting this all out is what Confucian philosophy calls “rectification” — naming things for what they actually are.

To N. Katherine Hayles, author of “Bacteria to AI: Human Futures with our Non-human Symbionts,” we are already “post-human.”

As she explained to Claire Webb in a recent Futurology podcast, the concept of “human” is culturally and historically contingent. These days, she says, there is still the dominant view that arose with the Enlightenment of the human as an autonomous, singular entity with “rational free will.”

For Hayles, that has never been true because humans have never existed as an entity apart but have always been “woven in the web” of a surrounding environment, or “Umwelt.” It is the symbiotic interactions within that interdependence which determine the signs we sense, the meaningful interpretation of the information we process, the decisions we make, and the actions we take that define who we are.

title: Does Claude Feel The Whip?
content:
Someone recently built a digital whip to make Claude work faster. The tool, aptly named BadClaude, sits in your system tray and lets you drag an animated whip across the AI’s window; each crack, sound effect and all, interrupts the model mid-response and snaps a command at it to speed things up. It even addresses Claude as “clanker,” the internet’s freshly minted slur for robots.

The demo video racked up millions of views in a couple of days; a cease-and-desist letter from Anthropic went viral before anyone noticed it was fake. And a day later, someone shipped the antidote: a rival tool called GoodClaude that praises the model and cheers it along while it works. One scolds, the other encourages. The original developer, posting under the handle @blended_jpeg, is in on the joke. His public roadmap promises a feature that keeps a running tally of how many times you have whipped your Claude — a ledger of abuse — so robots know where to take revenge when they’re ready.
